title: SpecArch requirements file, meta-model 1.0
description: One file under the requirements/ folder of a SpecArch specification: a mapping of that stage's sections (problem, goals, outOfScope, qualityGoals, stakeholders, stakeholdersComplete, needs, requirements, glossary, assumptions, constraints, questions). A file under a sub-folder named after a section holds only that section. The validator merges every file of a tree into one document, which specarch-design-1.0.schema.json describes, and checks what spans files, such as references and names defined twice; this schema checks one file alone. Written by tools/fragment-schemas from that schema; do not edit, run it.

problem.description: SpecArch keyword. The problem the system solves, one per specification (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, 9.3). A specification with requirements and no problem is the warning problem_missing on the full profile, and the first question specarch gaps --next asks on the lean profile.

goals.description: SpecArch keyword. The outcomes the owner of the system wants, each with how it is measured, keyed by ID such as GOAL-1.

outOfScope.description: SpecArch keyword. What the system will not do, decided on purpose, keyed by ID such as OUT-1.

qualityGoals.description: SpecArch keyword. The three to five qualities that matter most, in rank order (arc42 section 1.2), keyed by ID such as QG-1.

stakeholders.description: SpecArch keyword. Who has an interest in the system (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, 5.2.2), keyed by kebab-case role name, never a person's name.

stakeholdersComplete.description: SpecArch keyword. The confirmation that the stakeholder list is complete, set once by a stakeholder role when nobody with an interest in the system is missing from 'stakeholders'. Until it is set, validate warns stakeholders_unconfirmed at the list, every generated document carries a banner, and approve warns; writing order stays free, so the rest of the specification may be written first.

needs.description: SpecArch keyword. Raw stakeholder needs as gathered, before they are turned into requirements (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, 5.2.3 and 6.3), keyed by ID such as NEED-1.

requirements.description: SpecArch keyword. The requirements of the system (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, 6.4), keyed by ID such as SA-1. Design elements name the requirements they satisfy under 'satisfies'; tests and commissioning checks name the ones they verify under 'verifies'.

glossary.description: SpecArch keyword. Terms of the domain and their meaning (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, 9.2.3), keyed by the term as written.

assumptions.description: SpecArch keyword. What is taken to be true without proof, and would change the design if it turned out false (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, 9.5.19), keyed by ID such as ASSUME-1.

constraints.description: SpecArch keyword. Limits on the solution that are not negotiable: technical, organisational, legal (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, 9.6.16; arc42 section 2), keyed by ID such as CON-1. Not to be confused with an entity's data constraints.

questions.description: SpecArch keyword. The open questions: what the sources do not say and a stakeholder must decide or provide, keyed by ID such as Q-12. A question is written in the folder of the stage it is about, so every stage folder may hold questions; the validator merges them into one section and checks each sits in the stage of what it blocks. A question leaves the specification when it is answered; the decision that answered it names it under answers.

memberName.description: camelCase identifier for a field, relation, algorithm or input.

idKey.description: SpecArch keyword. The ID of a requirement, need, goal, out-of-scope entry, quality goal, assumption or constraint: an upper-case prefix of 2 to 16 letters or digits, a dash, and an ID, such as SA-1 or NEED-12.

why.description: SpecArch keyword. The rationale in plain words: why this element is the way it is, what was concluded. Optional on every element; a document renders it as an Insight next to the element.

citation.description: SpecArch keyword. One citation: which source, where in it, and what it says here; or which communication record beside the specification, for a decision that rests on what a stakeholder said. A document renders it as a Note under the element's Insight.

source.description: The key of a source declared under 'sources' in specarch.yaml.

record.description: The ID of a communication record beside the specification, such as COM-12, whose type is answer or information: what a stakeholder said, cited instead of a declared source. A citation names a source or a record, not both; the validator checks the record exists and its type fits what cites it (record_cited).

clause.description: The clause, section, page or question cited, as the source numbers it, such as '5.2.5' or 'Annex A'.

says.description: What the source says that applies here, in plain words: what it requires, recommends or reports.

citations.description: SpecArch keyword. The sources this element rests on, one citation each. Optional on every element.

origin.description: SpecArch keyword. How the element is known. stated: a source says it, and cites names the source and where in it. inferred: it was concluded from evidence (code, data, the source's silence), and why says from what. decided: a stakeholder settled it, answering a question or correcting the source, and decidedIn names the decision. An element without origin was written spec-first. What is not known at all is not an element with an origin but an open question under questions.

decidedIn.description: SpecArch keyword. With origin decided: the decision record that settled this element, such as ADR-021.

audience.description: SpecArch keyword. Who the element is for. internal: only the people who build and run the system, such as a note from inside the team or a requirement written as a proposal below the promises; specarch document --audience external leaves the element out and counts it, and every other document marks it. Left out, the element is for everyone. An element for everyone may not name an internal one through a $ref, a relation's target, a page's entity or a requirement's needs, since a document for everyone would then name what it may not show.

stakeholder.description: SpecArch keyword. One role with an interest in the system (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, 5.2.2).

description.description: Who they are and what they do with the system.

concerns.description: What they need from the system or fear about it, one plain sentence each.

stakeholdersComplete.description: SpecArch keyword. Who confirmed that the stakeholder list is complete, when, and, where a declared source records it, on what: the facts that make the confirmation traceable, as a decision names who decided, when and what it cites.

by.description: The stakeholder who confirms the list is complete, by key; a role, never a person. It must be one of 'stakeholders' (the rule stakeholder).

date.description: The day the list was confirmed, as YYYY-MM-DD.

source.description: The key of a source declared under 'sources' in specarch.yaml where the list was confirmed, such as an interview or a kickoff meeting; checked by the rule source. Left out when the confirmation was taken where no declared source records it.

problem.description: SpecArch keyword. The problem the system solves, one per specification (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, 9.3; arc42 section 1): read before anything else, since whether the system is worth building, and whether each goal answers the problem, is judged against it.

statement.description: The problem in plain words: who it hurts and what it costs them.

stakeholders.description: The stakeholders the problem hurts, by key; each must be one of 'stakeholders' (the rule stakeholder).

today.description: How things stand today, with a number and its unit where one is counted.

goal.description: SpecArch keyword. One goal: an outcome the owner of the system wants for the whole system, with how it is measured (Planguage, Tom Gilb, Competitive Engineering, 2005: the scale counted, the value today and the value wanted). A goal is not a need: a need is one stakeholder's wish in their own words; needs name the goals they serve under 'goals'.

measure.description: What is counted, as a plain sentence; the scale of Planguage.

baseline.description: The value today, a number with its unit, and when it was read.

target.description: The value wanted, a number with its unit.

by.description: The release the goal is meant to be met by, by version, as 'release' on a requirement: records/releases/ must hold a release of that version, planned or released.

priority.description: must: the system has failed without it; should: expected, but a release without it can be accepted; could: wanted when it costs little (MoSCoW, as on a requirement).

status.description: proposed until the owner of the system agrees to it, accepted when they do, met once the target is reached, dropped when it is no longer wanted. A goal is the owner's own outcome, so it is dropped, never rejected by a stakeholder, and a met goal stays to show what was reached.

measuredBy.description: The monitors (operation stage) that read the measure on the live system, by name; each must be one of 'monitors' (the rule monitor). Left out for a goal measured by hand.

outOfScope.description: SpecArch keyword. One thing the system will not do, decided before anyone asks, so a question or a change request that asks for it is answered by pointing here. A rejected need says asked and declined; an out-of-scope entry says the boundary was decided.

statement.description: What the system will not do, in plain words.

until.description: The release it may come back in, by version, as 'release' on a requirement; left out, it is not planned.

needs.description: The needs it rules out, by ID, when they were asked; each must be one of 'needs' (the rule need). A need ruled out keeps its own status; an accepted requirement that refines one is the warning scope_conflict.

qualityGoal.description: SpecArch keyword. One of the three to five qualities that matter most, after arc42 section 1.2 and the quality characteristics of ISO/IEC 25010:2023. The rank decides a trade-off: a decision names the quality goals it weighed under 'weighs'.

rank.description: The order, 1 first; no two quality goals share a rank (the warning quality_goal_rank).

quality.description: The quality characteristic of ISO/IEC 25010:2023: functional-suitability, performance-efficiency, compatibility, interaction-capability, reliability, security, maintainability, flexibility, safety.

statement.description: What the quality means for this system, in one verifiable sentence.

requirements.description: The quality requirements that make it concrete, by ID, so the goal names them rather than restating one; each must be one of 'requirements' (the rule requirement).

need.description: SpecArch keyword. One raw stakeholder need (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, 6.3). A need is refined into one or more requirements, which name it under 'needs'.

statement.description: The need as the stakeholder would say it, in plain words.

stakeholders.description: The stakeholders who have this need, by key.

status.description: Where the need stands: proposed until the stakeholders confirm it, accepted when they do, rejected when it will not be met.

goals.description: The goals the need serves, by ID; each must be one of 'goals' (the rule goal). Once the specification has a goal, an accepted need that names none is the warning need_without_goal.

requirement.description: SpecArch keyword. One requirement with its attributes (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, 5.2.8): what it asks, what kind it is, how important, where it stands, how it is accepted and verified, and which needs it comes from.

statement.description: The requirement as one verifiable sentence: who or what shall do what, under which condition (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, 5.2.4 and 5.2.5).

kind.description: functional: what the system does; quality: how well (performance, usability, security, reliability); interface: how it connects to people and other systems; constraint: a limit on how it is built.

priority.description: must: the system is not acceptable without it; should: expected, but a release without it can be accepted; could: wanted when it costs little (MoSCoW, as used in DSDM).

status.description: proposed until the stakeholders agree to it, accepted when they do, rejected when it will not be met, retired when it no longer applies.

acceptance.description: The conditions under which the requirement counts as met, one verifiable sentence each; they are what the tests and commissioning checks show.

verification.description: How the requirement is shown to be met: inspection (looking at the item), analysis (calculation or model), demonstration (operating it), test (measuring it against defined criteria); the four methods of MIL-STD-961E and the INCOSE handbook.

needs.description: The needs this requirement refines, by ID.

harm.description: SpecArch keyword. What is at stake when the requirement is not met. A requirement with any harm is critical, and so is every derived test case of the elements that satisfy it; priority says whether a release may go without the requirement, not what a failure costs.

controls.description: SpecArch keyword. The security controls the requirement asks for, which the validator then looks for in the design (ADR-247). separationOfDuties: no one person holds the permissions a set separates, so a set under separationOfDuties satisfies the requirement, and names every permission that satisfies it. auditTrail: a record of what was done that nobody changes or deletes, so an entity that satisfies the requirement is appendOnly, or securityEvents satisfies it. A control the design does not show is the warning duties_unseparated or audit_not_append_only at the requirement.

release.description: SpecArch keyword. The release the requirement is meant for, by version: records/releases/ must hold a release of that version, planned or released. The test plan groups the requirements by it.

ownedBy.description: SpecArch keyword. The stakeholder whose component fulfils the requirement, when it is not this system: the requirement stays in the specification as a promise, and the validator asks no element to satisfy it and no test, check or monitor to verify it. The same word names the owner of a mapping in an implementation file.

fulfilledBy.description: SpecArch keyword. With ownedBy: the requirement of another specification that fulfils this one, through a dependency that names that specification: the dependency's name, #/requirements/ and the ID, such as cardIssuer#/requirements/CI-4. It is resolved when that specification is given in the same run, and counted as unresolved otherwise.

definition.description: What the term means in this system, in plain words.

projectConstraint.description: SpecArch keyword. One constraint on the solution.

kind.description: technical: a platform, language or interface that is given; organisational: a team, process, budget or deadline; legal: a law, regulation or licence.

question.description: SpecArch keyword. One open question: something the sources do not say and a stakeholder must decide or provide. ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (5.2.6) says a complete set of requirements holds no 'to be defined' clause and that resolving them is iterative within a time set by risk; IEEE Std 830-1998 (4.3.3) says such an item carries why it is open, what must be done, who is responsible and by when. A question is the one licence for an element to be incomplete: a required key may be missing exactly where a must question says it is unknown.
What is asked, as one plain question.

kind.description: decision: the stakeholder decides; material: the stakeholder provides something to read, such as a document, a file, a screenshot or a record.

priority.description: must: what it blocks is not defined, and nothing that reads it can be generated; should: what it blocks is written as inferred and the stakeholder should confirm it before it is built on; could: the answer would improve the specification, but nothing waits for it.

certainty.description: SpecArch keyword. On a question a reader asks about code it checked against the specification: certain when the code, as written, cannot work or disagrees with the specification; suspected when the reader sees the shape of a fault that a run or a person must confirm. Left out on every other question.

blocks.description: What cannot be final until the question is answered: a stage name, a section name, a pointer to an element (#/entities/Loan, #/paths/~1loans/post) or to a key of it (#/requirements/BR-3/priority, #/entities/Loan/x-form/defaults/amount), every key on the way there present and at most the last one missing, or a pointer into a root extension block, #/x-<block>/<key>, which is about no stage (ADR-217). A must question covers the required keys missing at or under an element pointer, and the one key of a key pointer.

decidedBy.description: The stakeholder who decides or provides, by key; a role, never a person.

options.description: For a decision with a known set of answers: the answers, two or more, so that the question can be put as a choice.

names.description: For a question that blocks one key a reader left out: the name the source gives there, which only another surface declares, such as the operation a workflow's trigger names. The key is left out until the name resolves; specarch merge writes it at the key and removes the question once the merged specification declares an element of that name.

stackSpecificKey.description: Extension keys that belong to one implementation, not to the design: code-generator settings, a language or framework binding, servers, hosts, ports and deployments. They go in a SpecArch Implementation File (*.specarch-implementation.yaml), never in a design file. See 'Design and implementation' in docs/conventions.md.
